what_its_for: This medicine is used to treat certain types of cancer, including breast cancer that has spread to other parts of the body, non-small cell lung cancer (when used with another medicine called carboplatin), and pancreatic cancer (when used with another medicine called gemcitabine). It works by stopping cancer cells from growing and dividing.
how_to_take: This medicine is given to you by a nurse or doctor through a needle placed in your vein (called an IV infusion). You will NOT give this medicine to yourself at home. Each infusion usually takes about 30 minutes. Your doctor or nurse will tell you exactly how many treatments you will need and how often you will come in for them. Do not miss any scheduled appointments. Tell your nurse right away if you feel any burning, pain, or swelling near the IV site during your infusion.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your body size (height and weight), the type of cancer you have, and how well your kidneys and liver are working. Common schedules include once every 3 weeks, or once a week for 3 weeks followed by 1 week off. Your dose may be lowered or your treatment may be delayed if you have certain side effects such as low blood cell counts or nerve problems. Never try to change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given at a clinic or hospital, your healthcare team will schedule your infusions for you. If you need to miss or reschedule an appointment, call your doctor or clinic as soon as possible. Do not try to double up on doses. Your doctor will decide the safest time to reschedule your next treatment.
storage: You do not need to store this medicine at home because it is prepared and given by healthcare professionals. The medicine is kept as a powder in vials in a refrigerator or at room temperature at the clinic. Once it is mixed (reconstituted) by the pharmacy or nurse, it should be used within a certain number of hours. If you have any leftover supplies at home for any reason, keep them out of reach of children and ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of them.
what_to_avoid: Avoid being around people who are sick or have infections, since this medicine can lower your ability to fight germs. Wash your hands often. Avoid cutting yourself or getting injuries, as this medicine can also lower your blood's ability to clot. Do not get any vaccines (shots) without checking with your doctor first, especially live vaccines. Avoid alcohol, as it may make some side effects worse. Women of childbearing age should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after the last dose, because this medicine can harm an unborn baby. Men should also use birth control during treatment and for at least 3 months after. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the nearest emergency room right away if you experience any of the following: fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, chills, or signs of infection; unusual bruising or bleeding; severe numbness, tingling, or pain in your hands or feet; shortness of breath or chest pain; severe allergic reaction (hives, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing, dizziness); severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that you cannot control; yellowing of your skin or eyes; sores in your mouth that make it hard to eat or drink; or any new or worsening symptoms that concern you. Also call your doctor before your next treatment if you notice your hands or feet feel numb or weak, as your dose may need to be adjusted.
when_it_works: This medicine works right away at the cellular level to stop cancer cells from dividing, but it may take several weeks or months of treatment before you or your doctor can see or measure an improvement in your cancer. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular exams, blood tests, and imaging scans (such as CT scans). Do not stop treatment on your own even if you do not feel better right away. Keep all follow-up appointments so your doctor can track how well the treatment is working.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: This medicine can cause serious harm to an unborn baby. Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant during treatment. Do not breastfeed while using this medicine. Older adults (age 65 and over): Older patients may be more likely to experience certain side effects such as weakness, numbness in the hands and feet, and low blood cell counts. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Liver problems: If your liver is not working well, your dose may need to be lowered. Tell your doctor about any history of liver disease. Children: The safety and effectiveness of this medicine in children have not been established. Always tell your doctor and pharmacist about all other medicines, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are taking, because some medicines can interact with paclitaxel protein-bound particles.
